processing: Made as sencha, often deep-steamed, with gentle rolling because the leaf is tender; also used for kabusecha and tencha.
harvest_season: Early budding: first flush in mid-April in Kagoshima; low yields and frost damage keep plantings small.
appearance_dry: Fine, slightly broken, intensely green needles with a soft texture.
appearance_wet: Very tender, small, bright green leaves that turn to a soft mush.
taste_profile: Thick, sweet and deeply umami with almost no astringency, a milky softness and a mild green aroma; the reason it is nicknamed 'natural gyokuro'.

brewing.notes: Cool water and a fine mesh; it extracts quickly and is nearly impossible to make bitter at 60–70 °C. Cold brew is where it shines.

vintage_note: A rare single-cultivar lot sold as the current year's first flush by a limited number of farms, mainly in Kagoshima, and often sold out by summer; a few Shizuoka and Miyazaki growers make it as a speciality. It is not aged and should be drunk within the year.
description:
Asatsuyu is the cultivar nicknamed 'natural gyokuro': a selection from old Uji seedling bushes, registered in 1953, that makes a sweet, thick, umami-rich tea with almost no astringency even without shading. It is also awkward to grow, low-yielding and prone to frost, which is why it has stayed a speciality rather than a mainstay and why most of it now grows in Kagoshima, with a few committed growers in Shizuoka and Miyazaki.

Its tender leaf is usually deep-steamed and rolled gently, which produces fine, slightly broken needles of an intense green and an opaque, soupy cup. It buds early, so it is often among the first shincha of the year, and it is the parent of both Saemidori and Yutaka Midori, which means its sweetness is in a large share of modern Kagoshima tea even where its name is not.

Brew it cool, 60–70 °C, 5 g for 150 ml for a minute with a fine mesh; it extracts quickly and is nearly impossible to make bitter at that temperature. The cup is thick, sweet and deeply savoury with a milky softness and a mild green aroma, closer to kabusecha than to ordinary sencha; the second steep is almost instant, and a cold brew is where it really shines. The only mistake is hot water, which flattens the sweetness without adding much.

It is sold as a labelled single-cultivar sencha of the current year's first flush by a limited number of farms, mostly in Kagoshima, at a premium for the rarity, and it is often sold out by summer. Look for an intense green colour in the dry leaf and a cloudy cup. Store it like sencha and drink it within the year.

Taste it beside its daughter Saemidori: the family resemblance is obvious, and so is the extra vigour the breeders added.
history:
Asatsuyu was registered in 1953 as Japanese tea cultivar No. 2, grown from the seed of a tea plant found in Uji, the gyokuro country. Its nickname, natural gyokuro, comes from the way it tastes: sweet and savoury like shaded tea, though grown in the sun.

The cultivar never became a mainstay. It yields less than Yabukita and suffers badly from frost, and breeders turned to it for its flavour instead. Yutakamidori was selected from an Asatsuyu seedling, and Saemidori comes from it as well, so its character reaches well beyond the tea sold under its own name.
